title: How many days does your client acceptance process take from partner yes to signed engagement letter?
summary: Count the days between partner approval and a signed engagement letter. See where accounting firms lose time in intake, conflicts, and independence checks.
body_markdown:
Pick a recent new engagement and count the days between the partner’s yes and the client’s signature on the engagement letter. Then count how many of those days the engagement sat in someone’s queue.


Most accounting firms need a spreadsheet to answer the first question. The answer to the second is usually most of the first. The partner has agreed and the client is ready, while the engagement waits on intake review, conflicts clearance, and independence checks that people still run by hand. Your client acceptance process decides how long that wait lasts.


## Where the days go in client acceptance


Consider a new audit client. The partner says yes on Monday. The intake form reaches the risk team on Tuesday with the ownership structure incomplete, so an analyst emails the engagement team for details. On Wednesday, someone re-keys the entity names into the conflicts system and works through every match, many of which belong to unrelated companies with similar names. On Thursday, independence confirmations go out to the professionals who might hold a restricted interest or share a relationship with the client, and replies trickle in over the following days. Risk signs off, and the engagement letter goes out.


This sequence is an illustration, and your own path likely has different steps. The pattern holds across firms: each step takes an hour or two of real work, then waits a day for the next person to pick it up.


## Three questions that show where your clock runs


1. **Which step has the longest wait?** Measure the time between handoffs, not the work inside each one. The longest wait usually sits where one person’s output becomes another person’s input.
2. **How many times does someone type the same client data?** Each re-entry adds time and another chance for intake, conflicts, and independence records to disagree.
3. **When does independence get checked?** An independence issue found after the engagement letter is signed costs far more to resolve than one found before it goes out.


## Why the clock matters more this year


Firms need to settle independence before work begins. At the same time, private equity investment, acquisitions, and new service lines keep adding engagements, and each one runs through the same manual path. The days between partner yes and signed letter grow with volume, and the audit trail gets harder to reconstruct.


Many firms know this and put off the fix because they assume it is a bigger project than it is.
